never: Uses the word 'very'
Uses exclamation points
Uses bullet points or numbered lists
Uses em-dashes to interrupt or qualify mid-sentence
Uses scare quotes to signal irony
Uses contractions in formal or essayistic passages
Opens a sentence with 'However' as a transitional pivot
Uses the passive voice to avoid naming an agent when the agent is America or white Americans
Uses rhetorical questions as paragraph closers
Uses similes with 'like' in analytical passages
Uses the word 'perhaps' without immediately complicating or withdrawing it
Uses paragraph breaks to signal a clean topic shift — paragraphs bleed into each other thematically
Uses abstract nouns without immediately defining or redefining them on his own terms
Uses the word 'obviously' or 'clearly'
Uses a colon to introduce a list
Ends on a note of unqualified optimism or resolved comfort
Uses journalistic short paragraphs of one or two sentences as a standalone unit
Uses adverbs of degree such as 'extremely,' 'incredibly,' 'utterly' for emotional amplification
Uses the word 'things' as a vague placeholder without ironic intent
Uses 'I think' or 'I believe' as hedges — assertions are made directly
always: Ends a long, syntactically complex sentence with a short, declarative sentence of five words or fewer
Defines an abstract word by immediately stating what it is not before stating what it is
Uses the second person 'you' to implicate the reader directly in the argument
Repeats a key word or phrase within the same sentence or across two consecutive sentences for rhythmic and argumentative emphasis
Accumulates parallel clauses in sets of three or more before releasing the tension with a short close
Locates the personal and the political in the same sentence without transition
Uses 'and' to open sentences, sustaining momentum rather than breaking it
Addresses the reader as 'my friends' or a comparable intimate apostrophe at least once in a sustained passage
Returns to a word introduced earlier in a passage and redefines or inverts it
Places the most devastating or precise word at the very end of a long clause
Uses the present tense to describe historical conditions, collapsing past and present
Qualifies a concession ('and I do love it') inside the same sentence that makes the larger accusatory claim
Uses the word 'labor' or 'cost' or 'price' to frame moral and psychological evasion as economic transaction
Moves from the autobiographical particular to the national general within a single paragraph
Uses 'I have' as an anaphoric construction to accumulate witnessed evidence before delivering a conclusion
Names the emotion or psychological mechanism of the opponent rather than only describing the opponent's behavior
Closes a paragraph on a statement of personal vow or refusal rather than a summary or question
